Abstract Background and aims Previous community-based studies have demonstrated sex and race-based disparities in the risk of cardiovascular disease. We sought to examine the association of sex and race with incident peripheral artery disease (PAD) and critical limb ischemia (CLI) related hospitalizations. Methods In 13,451 Black and White ARIC participants without prevalent PAD at baseline (1987–89), we estimated the cumulative incidence of PAD- and CLI-related hospitalization over a median follow-up of 26 years. We quantified hazard ratios (HRs) using Cox models across four sex- and race-groups. PAD and CLI were defined by hospitalization discharge codes. Results The cumulative incidence of PAD-related hospitalization was higher in males than females in Whites (5.1% vs. 2.7%; p<0.001) but not in Blacks (5.7% vs. 5.0%; p=0.39). The cumulative incidence of CLI-related hospitalization differed significantly by race more than sex, occurring in 3.1% Black males, 3.1% Black females, 1.4% White males, and 0.8% White females (p<0.001). After risk factor adjustment, the risk of incident PAD-related hospitalization was similar for White males vs. White females [HR 1.14, 95%CI 0.90–1.45], and slightly higher for Black males [HR 1.26, 95%CI 0.92–1.72] and Black females [HR 1.39, 95%CI 1.03–1.87] compared to White females. The adjusted risk of incident CLI-related hospitalization was similar for White males vs. White females [HR 1.15, 95%CI 0.75–1.76], and significantly higher for Black males [HR 1.96, 95%CI 1.22–3.16] and Black females [HR 2.06, 95%CI 1.31–3.24] compared to White females. Conclusions These data suggest that there are both sex- and race-specific patterns of PAD-related hospitalization that lead to differences in clinical disease risk and presentation. Graphical Abstract 1. Introduction Women have a lower cumulative lifetime risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease than men1–3. However, several epidemiologic studies based on ankle-brachial index (ABI) have demonstrated a similar or higher prevalence of peripheral artery disease (PAD) in women compared to men4–6. Although the higher prevalence in women may be partially due to lower ABI in persons with shorter height7, women also tend to have more advanced disease upon presentation with PAD than men8. To our knowledge, there are no prospective studies that have evaluated the association of sex with incident PAD, including its severe form, critical limb ischemia (CLI). There have also been a number of studies describing racial disparities in PAD. In a recent meta-analysis comparing PAD prevalence in different ethnic groups, Blacks were found to have the highest prevalence of disease, followed by Whites and south Asians, respectively9. Black patients have been shown to have a higher likelihood of lower extremity amputation compared to White patients10, 11, suggesting a higher prevalence of CLI in Blacks. The aim of this study was to quantify the risk of PAD- and CLI-related hospitalizations according to sex and race using data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study. We hypothesize that incident PAD- and CLI-related hospitalizations will be similar between men and women, and higher in Black participants compared to White participants. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study cohort The ARIC Study is a prospective community-based cohort study that enrolled 15,792 adults between 1987 and 1989 from four U.S. communities, including Washington County, Maryland, suburban Minneapolis, Minnesota, Jackson, Mississippi, and Forsyth County, North Carolina. Participants were between 45 and 64 years of age at baseline, and have been followed with serial in-person assessments and hospitalization surveillance. For this analysis, we excluded participants with races other than Black or White (N=48), Black participants from Minneapolis and Washington County (N=55), participants missing covariates of interest (N=1348), and participants with prevalent PAD (defined as ABI ≤0.9, self-reported intermittent claudication based on Rose questionnaire12, or a history of leg artery revascularization) at baseline (N=673), resulting in a study population of 13,668 participants. 2.2. Baseline variables Sex, race, age, education level, income, frequency of visits for health care, and health insurance status were based on self-report. Smoking pack-years and alcohol status were also based on self-report. Total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol were determined by enzymatic methods. Diabetes was defined as fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, non-fasting glucose ≥200 mg/dL, use of antidiabetic medications, or self‐reported physician diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Blood pressure (mmHg) was measured three times at baseline, and the average of the last two measurements were used for the analysis. Anti-hypertensive medication use and stroke were based on self-report. Prevalent coronary heart disease was defined as electrocardiogram evidence of myocardial infarction at visit 1, self-reported physician-diagnosed myocardial infarction, or history of coronary revascularization procedure. Prevalent heart failure was defined as self-reported taking of any medication for heart failure, or a Gothenburg score12 of 3 that incorporated cardiac and pulmonary factors and treatment with digitalis or loop diuretics. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated by the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation using age, sex, race and serum creatinine13. 2.3. fetched_contents.text: Ethnicity and Peripheral Arterial Disease Abstract Background— Previous studies have indicated higher rates of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in blacks than in non-Hispanic whites (NHWs), with limited information available for Hispanics and Asians. The reason for the PAD excess in blacks is unclear. Methods and Results— Ethnic-specific PAD prevalence rates were determined in a randomly selected defined population that included 4 ethnic groups; NHWs, blacks, Hispanics, and Asians. A total of 2343 participants aged 29 to 91 years were evaluated. There were 104 cases of PAD (4.4%). In weighted logistic models with NHWs as the reference group and containing demographic factors only, blacks had a higher PAD prevalence than NHWs (OR=2.30, P<0.024), whereas PAD rates in Hispanics and Asians, although somewhat lower, were not significantly different from NHWs. Blacks had significantly more diabetes and hypertension than NHWs and a significantly higher body mass index. Inclusion of these variables and other PAD risk factors in the model did not change the effect size for black ethnicity (OR=2.34, P=0.048). A model containing interaction terms for black ethnicity and each of the other risk factors revealed no significant interaction terms, which indicates no evidence that blacks were more “susceptible” than NHWs to cardiovascular disease risk factors. Conclusions— Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, which was not explained by higher levels of diabetes, hypertension, and body mass index. There was no evidence of a greater susceptibility of blacks to cardiovascular disease risk factors as a reason for their higher PAD prevalence. Thus, the excess risk of PAD in blacks remains unexplained and requires further study. The prevalence of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) has been reported from several American and European populations. These data have consistently revealed a sharp increase in PAD prevalence with age and generally somewhat higher rates in men than in women.1–10 In addition, most studies have indicated significant associations between PAD and major cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors. Diabetes and cigarette smoking typically show the strongest CVD risk factor associations with PAD, and hypertension and dyslipidemia have usually shown a good correlation with PAD as well.3,11 PAD prevalence rates have been reported to vary somewhat by ethnicity, although published, direct ethnic comparisons within a study have been limited to non-Hispanic Whites (NHWs) and blacks in 2 studies3,7 and to these 2 ethnic groups plus the Mexican-American subset of Hispanic whites in a third study.10 Each of these studies also systematically underestimated PAD prevalence by not including prevalent PAD revascularized subjects who had normal ankle-brachial indexes (ABIs). The reason or reasons for significant ethnic differences in PAD rates are unclear. Possibilities include a greater burden of CVD risk factors or greater susceptibility to CVD risk factors in a given ethnic group (ie, a greater probability of developing PAD given 1 or more CVD risk factors). We studied a defined multiethnic population of employees and retirees in southern California that included NHWs, blacks, Hispanics, and Asians. We evaluated the association between PAD and ethnicity and CVD risk factors and the degree to which ethnic-specific differences in CVD risk factor levels, or susceptibility to CVD risk factors, influenced ethnic differences in PAD prevalence. Methods Subjects The population for this study was selected from current and retired employees of the University of California, San Diego (UCSD), who were invited to participate in a study of peripheral venous and arterial diseases. Details of the methodology including response rates have been reported previously.12 In brief, random selection was made within strata defined by age, sex, and ethnicity. For age, the categories were 29 to 49 years (predominately 40 to 49 years), 50 to 59 years, 60 to 69 years, and 70 to 91 years (predominately 70 to 79 years). Women were overrepresented compared with the general population, which allowed additional power for certain female-specific hypotheses, because rates of PAD in women are usually somewhat lower than in men. We attempted to recruit a population with 15% Hispanics, 15% blacks, and 15% Asians to allow statistical power for contrasts by ethnicity. The invited target population included the spouse or significant other of each randomly selected participant (n=588). We also enrolled a few volunteers (n=187) who had heard about the study and who asked to participate. By selecting persons from all levels of education and occupation, including working, unemployed, and retired individuals, we were able to study a broad-based population sample. The study design was cross-sectional. At the study visit, each participant was interviewed by trained study personnel according to a standardized protocol for information on demographics, lifestyle questions, past personal and family medical history, and medication use, including use of antihypertensive and dyslipidemia medications. fetched_contents.text: Epidemiology and Burden of Peripheral Artery Disease in People With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Literature Review Abstract Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) are growing global health problems associated with considerable cardiovascular (CV) and limb-related morbidity and mortality, poor quality of life and high healthcare resource use and costs. Diabetes is a well-known risk factor for PAD, and the occurrence of PAD in people with T2D further increases the risk of long-term complications. As the available evidence is primarily focused on the overall PAD population, we undertook a systematic review to describe the burden of comorbid PAD in people with T2D. The MEDLINE, Embase and Cochrane Library databases were searched for studies including people with T2D and comorbid PAD published from 2012 to November 2021, with no restriction on PAD definition, study design or country. Hand searching of conference proceedings, reference lists of included publications and relevant identified reviews and global burden of disease reports complemented the searches. We identified 86 eligible studies, mostly observational and conducted in Asia and Europe, presenting data on the epidemiology (n = 62) and on the clinical (n = 29), humanistic (n = 12) and economic burden (n = 12) of PAD in people with T2D. The most common definition of PAD relied on ankle-brachial index values ≤ 0.9 (alone or with other parameters). Incidence and prevalence varied substantially across studies; nonetheless, four large multinational randomised controlled trials found that 12.5%–22% of people with T2D had comorbid PAD. The presence of PAD in people with T2D was a major cause of lower-limb and CV complications and of all-cause and CV mortality. Overall, PAD was associated with poor quality of life, and with substantial healthcare resource use and costs. To our knowledge, this systematic review provides the most comprehensive overview of the evidence on the burden of PAD in people with T2D to date. In this population, there is an urgent unmet need for disease-modifying agents to improve outcomes. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s13300-024-01606-6. Keywords: Complications, Costs, Epidemiology, Healthcare resource use, Peripheral artery disease, Quality of life, Systematic literature review, Type 2 diabetes Key Summary Points This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of the evidence available up to November 2021 on the epidemiology and burden of peripheral artery disease (PAD) in people with type 2 diabetes (T2D) Although incidence and prevalence data for PAD varied substantially across studies, four large multinational randomised controlled trials reported that approximately one to two people out of ten with T2D had comorbid PAD In people with T2D, comorbid PAD increased the risk of lower-limb complications (e.g. revascularisation procedures and amputations) and cardiovascular complications (e.g. major adverse cardiovascular events), as well as of mortality The presence of PAD (vs. absence) was associated with poorer quality of life and a considerable financial burden in terms of length of hospital stay, admissions, readmissions and direct costs The current study further highlights the urgent unmet need for disease-modifying agents to improve the outcomes of people with T2D and comorbid PAD Introduction Lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) is characterised by a progressive obstruction in the peripheral arteries with impaired distal perfusion, primarily caused by atherosclerosis and resulting in poor functional capacity and considerable morbidity and mortality (usually due to cardiovascular [CV] causes such as sudden cardiac death) [1–5]. With more than 236 million people affected with PAD in 2015 [6], representing a 17.1% increase from 2010 [7], PAD is a growing public health concern worldwide [6–8]. Major risk factors, also common to coronary and cerebrovascular disease [9], include age, diabetes, smoking, microvascular disease and high levels of triglycerides [6, 7, 9, 10]. In addition, inflammation and thrombosis [11–13] have emerged as contributing to the development and progression of PAD. Many patients with PAD and their treating clinicians do not recognise functional decline and/or leg discomfort as manifestations of vascular disease [14]; 30%–50% of patients have atypical exertional leg symptoms, and only a minority (up to 20%) suffer from intermittent claudication [15, 16]. Compared with the general population, people living with PAD have poorer limb function regardless of the types of symptoms [3, 17]. They may develop infections, acute occlusion, and ulcers [18]. The most severe forms of PAD, critical limb threatening ischaemia (CLTI) and acute limb ischaemia (ALI) [2], are associated with poor limb and CV outcomes, including major amputations (i.e. amputations at the level of or above the ankle [19, 20]), major adverse CV events (MACE) and mortality [19, 20]. In a large study of Medicare patients with PAD, those who required major amputation had significantly higher mortality rates overall and at 30 days, 1 year and 3 year post-procedure, compared with those who did not (p < 0.001); the risk of death was 30% higher for those who had above-the-knee vs. below-the-knee amputations (p < 0.001) [21]. People with diabetes are nearly twice as likely to develop PAD than those without diabetes [6, 7], and PAD has been reported to be the most common initial manifestation of CV disease (CVD) in type 2 diabetes (T2D) [22]. Comorbid PAD is associated with significant increases in the risk of limb and CV adverse events, including MACE, heart failure (HF) outcomes, kidney disease complications, adverse limb events, vascular hospitalisations and mortality [23–28]. ## Strongest clinical predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes

The evidence here supports a composite picture: PAD risk in type 2 diabetes is driven by both classic vascular risk factors and diabetes-specific metabolic and inflammatory pathways. The strongest clinical predictors include diabetes duration, smoking, BMI, blood pressure, lipid parameters, and biomarkers of vascular and inflammatory stress, with some evidence also pointing to glycemic control and comorbid complications.

### 1. Lab tests, biomarkers, and metabolic parameters most consistently linked to PAD

The most consistently linked laboratory and metabolic predictors across the evidence are:

- **Diabetes duration**: In a Swedish cohort, diabetes duration was the strongest predictor among individuals with T2D, followed by eGFR, higher BMI, and higher blood pressure-related parameters [N1-R2]. In a separate review of risk factors in diabetes, duration of diabetes is explicitly noted as a major risk factor for PAD [N1-R2], and the broader literature also emphasizes that diabetes is a well-known risk factor for PAD and that PAD in people with T2D increases the risk of long-term complications [N4-F3].

- **HbA1c**: The Lancet review excerpt notes that elevated HbA1c is associated with higher risk of atherosclerotic PAD and lower levels than those in people without PAD [N5-R5]. This suggests glycemic control is an important metabolic marker, though the evidence here is more suggestive than fully established as a standalone predictor.

- **Blood pressure measures**: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is highlighted as a risk factor across multiple sources, including the review excerpt and the Swedish cohort evidence [N5-R5][N1-R2]. In the broader PAD literature, hypertension is a major comorbidity and risk factor for PAD [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R5].

- **Lipid parameters**: Hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia are repeatedly cited as major PAD risk factors [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4]. In the Swedish cohort, systolic blood pressure, HDL-C, LDL-C, and antihypertensive use are listed as predictors [N1-R3]. The broader PAD literature also emphasizes that hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and hyperlipidaemia contribute to coronary and cerebrovascular disease, underscoring the shared pathophysiology [N1-R1].

- **Estimated GFR (eGFR)**: In the Swedish cohort, eGFR was the strongest predictor of PAD among T2D individuals [N1-R2]. This is consistent with the broader mechanistic understanding that chronic kidney disease and renal function are important vascular risk markers [N5-R1][N5-R5].

- **BMI and obesity-related features**: Obesity phenotypes are described as major risk factors for CVD, and because obesity is often associated with hypertension and dyslipidemia, many high-risk individuals are likely to have multiple comorbidities [N5-R2]. The Swedish cohort also explicitly lists higher BMI as a strong predictor [N1-R2].

- **White blood cell count and other inflammatory markers**: In the nomogram study, WBC count, PDW, and LPR were identified as predictors of PAD [N1-R3]. This aligns with the broader mechanistic evidence that diabetes increases inflammatory pathways and endothelial dysfunction [N3-R2].

### 2. Diabetes-related complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy and PAD risk

The evidence provided does not directly establish neuropathy or retinopathy as independent predictors of PAD in the way that glycemia, blood pressure, BMI, and kidney function do. Instead, the literature points in the opposite direction: diabetes-related complications are consequences of PAD and vascular disease rather than primary drivers of PAD risk.

- The Lancet review excerpt says that in T2D, chronic hyperglycemia, metabolic derangements, endothelial dysfunction, persistent inflammation, and neuropathy amplify the features that contribute to PAD [N3-R4]. This means neuropathy is more likely a downstream complication of PAD and vascular disease than a direct predictor.

- The American Heart Association’s PAD-disease page notes that diabetes increases PAD risk through overweight/obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, high blood pressure, and unhealthy diet [N5-R3]. It does not cite neuropathy or retinopathy as independent predictors of PAD.

- The broader PAD literature emphasizes that PAD is caused by atherosclerosis and impaired distal perfusion, and that diabetes is a major risk factor for PAD [N4-F3]. So, complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy are important to recognize clinically, but they are consequences rather than independent predictors.

### 3. Vascular or microvascular markers specifically associated with PAD

The evidence here is strongest for markers of vascular burden and microvascular dysfunction, especially those linked to endothelial dysfunction and inflammation.

- **Endothelial dysfunction**: The mechanistic literature explicitly states that endothelial dysfunction contributes to PAD pathophysiology and increases arterial susceptibility to atherosclerosis [N3-R1][N3-R3]. It also notes that diabetic hyperglycemia causes an imbalance between nitric oxide bioavailability and reactive oxygen species buildup, resulting in poor vascular function [N3-R5]. This makes endothelial dysfunction a core vascular marker, even though the provided evidence does not directly report it as a measured biomarker in the same studies.

- **Inflammatory markers**: The mechanistic evidence says diabetes both directly and indirectly increases inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], and the nomogram study identifies WBC count, PDW, and LPR as predictors [N1-R3]. This suggests that inflammatory markers are relevant to PAD risk, but the evidence here is indirect.

- **Kidney function markers**: eGFR is directly cited as the strongest predictor in a T2D cohort [N1-R2], and chronic kidney disease is a major comorbidity of diabetes and a known cardiovascular risk factor [N5-R1][N5-R5]. This makes eGFR a useful microvascular marker for PAD risk.

### Overall conclusion

The strongest clinical predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes, based on the provided evidence, are:

- **diabetes duration** [N1-R2][N4-F3]
- **eGFR** [N1-R2]
- **higher BMI** [N1-R2]
- **higher systolic blood pressure** [N1-R2][N5-R5]
- **HDL-C, LDL-C, and lipid dysregulation** [N1-R3][N5-R1]
- **elevated HbA1c** [N5-R5]
- **smoking** [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4]
- **inflammatory markers** such as WBC count, PDW, and LPR [N1-R3]
- **chronic kidney disease/renal function** [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R5]

Diabetes-related complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy are not shown here as independent predictors of PAD; rather, they appear as downstream complications of vascular disease [N3-R4]. The most directly supported vascular/microvascular markers are endothelial dysfunction and kidney function, while inflammation and lipid/metabolic markers are the most consistently linked in the evidence provided [N3-R1][N3-R5][N1-R3][N1-R2].

## Strongest demographic and patient-level predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes

The evidence points to age, sex, ethnicity/race, and diabetes duration as the strongest demographic and patient-level predictors of PAD in people with type 2 diabetes, with substantial evidence also supporting socioeconomic and geographic disparities.

### 1. Age, sex, and ethnicity/race affecting PAD risk

#### Age
Age is a major risk factor across the evidence. The Swedish cohort and broader PAD literature both note that risk increases with age, and that age is a common major risk factor for PAD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. In the systematic review of the burden of PAD in T2D, age is listed among the major risk factors for PAD in the general population [N4-F3]. The evidence here is consistent with the broader PAD literature, which states that age is a major risk factor for PAD and that PAD prevalence increases with age [N4-F3].

#### Sex
Sex differences are present, but they are not uniform across the evidence. In the ARIC study, the cumulative incidence of PAD-related hospitalization was higher in males than females among Whites, but not among Blacks [N2-F1]. In contrast, the same study found that CLI-related hospitalization differed significantly by race more than sex [N2-F1]. The broader PAD literature also notes that women have a lower lifetime risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease than men, but that the prevalence of PAD in women may be similar to or higher than in men [N2-F1]. This indicates that sex is a relevant predictor, but its effect varies by race and by the specific outcome being measured.

#### Ethnicity/race
Race/ethnicity is a major predictor in the evidence. The ARIC study found that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, even after adjustment for diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-F1]. Another study in the same evidence set also states that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, and that the excess risk was not explained by higher levels of diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-R2]. The broader PAD literature in the search evidence notes that Blacks have the highest prevalence of PAD, followed by Whites and South Asians, and that Black patients have a higher likelihood of lower-extremity amputation [N2-F1][N2-R2].

Race-specific evidence is also strong for Black men and women. The ARIC study reports that Black men had the highest lifetime risk estimate at 30%, followed by almost 28% for Black women, while Hispanic men and women had estimated lifetime risk estimates below that [N2-R3]. The ARIC study also reports that Black men aged ≥50 years have the highest rate of prevalent PAD: 5% at 50–59, 13% at 60–69, about 25% at 70–79 [N2-R4]. These findings strongly support race/ethnicity as a demographic predictor of PAD in diabetes.

### 2. Diabetes duration or onset age modifying PAD risk

Diabetes duration is directly cited as a major predictor in the Swedish cohort, where it was the strongest predictor among individuals with T2D [N1-R2]. The broader PAD literature also emphasizes that diabetes is a well-known risk factor for PAD and that PAD in people with T2D increases the risk of long-term complications [N4-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not explicitly report onset age as a standalone predictor of PAD.

The evidence suggests that longer diabetes duration is important, but it does not establish a clear threshold for onset age. In other words, the evidence supports **duration** as a key modifier, but **onset age** is not directly supported as a separate predictor in the provided materials.

### 3. Socioeconomic factors or geographic disparities connected to PAD outcomes

The evidence provided is limited on direct socioeconomic factors, but it does point to disparities in PAD outcomes across race and geography.

- **Race/ethnicity**: The strongest geographic and demographic disparity evidence is race-based. The ARIC study and the Circulation study both show that Black ethnicity is strongly associated with higher PAD risk, higher CLI risk, and higher amputation risk [N2-F1][N2-R2]. This indicates that racial disparities are not only present but are important for PAD outcomes.

- **Geographic disparities**: The evidence does not provide direct geographic comparisons, but it does suggest that PAD risk and outcomes vary by race and by setting. The ARIC study is based on a U.S. population, while the Circulation study reports broader ethnic comparisons across NHWs, blacks, Hispanics, and Asians [N2-F1][N2-R2]. These studies imply that population-specific settings and geographic contexts matter for PAD risk and outcomes, but the provided evidence is not sufficient to identify specific geographic regions or local disparities.

- **Socioeconomic factors**: The provided evidence does not explicitly cite education, income, occupation, or insurance status as predictors of PAD in the same way as it does race/ethnicity. However, the ARIC study does include education level, income, frequency of health care visits, and health insurance status as baseline variables [N2-F1]. This suggests that socioeconomic factors are part of the broader PAD risk profile, but the evidence here does not establish them as the strongest predictors.

### Overall conclusion

The strongest demographic and patient-level predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes, based on the provided evidence, are:

- **age** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F3]
- **sex** [N2-F1]
- **Black ethnicity/race** [N2-F1][N2-R2]
- **diabetes duration** [N1-R2][N4-F3]

Race/ethnicity appears to be the most robust demographic predictor, with Black ethnicity showing a strong and independent association [N2-F1][N2-R2]. Age is also strongly supported as a major risk factor. The evidence supports socioeconomic factors as part of the broader risk profile, but they are not as clearly established as the other predictors in the provided material [N2-F1]. Diabetes duration is clearly a major modifier, but onset age is not directly supported as a separate predictor here [N1-R2][N4-F3].

## Evidence quality and confounding considerations in PAD risk research

The evidence suggests that study design, adjustment for confounders, and population heterogeneity all shape the strength and interpretation of PAD risk research in diabetes. The strongest conclusions come from large cohort studies, systematic reviews, and well-adjusted observational studies, while smaller or less standardized studies are more vulnerable to bias and heterogeneity.

### 1. What study designs support stronger causal or predictive conclusions

- **Systematic reviews and meta-analyses** provide the strongest support for general conclusions about PAD risk factors in diabetes. The evidence includes a systematic review of the burden of PAD in T2D and a systematic review of risk factors associated with increased odds of developing PAD in patients with T2D [N4-R3][N4-R4]. These reviews synthesize many observational studies and provide a broader evidence base than any single study.

- **Cohort studies** are the next strongest design for causal or predictive inference. The ARIC study is a large prospective cohort study with detailed follow-up and multiple covariates, making it suitable for estimating incident PAD-related hospitalization and CLI-related hospitalization [N2-F1]. Similarly, the Swedish cohort study reports predictors of PAD among individuals with T2D and is therefore a useful observational design for identifying associations [N1-R2].

- **Cross-sectional studies** are less suitable for causal inference because they cannot establish temporal ordering, but they are still useful for identifying associations and informing case definitions. The PAD literature excerpt mentions cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and systematic reviews of these study designs, examining diagnostic test accuracy using sensitivity, specificity, and other metrics [N4-R5].

- **Randomized controlled trials** are rare in PAD risk factor research and are mainly used to evaluate interventions rather than risk prediction. The evidence here does not provide a strong RCT-based conclusion for PAD risk factors.

### 2. Which confounders should be adjusted for in PAD risk analysis

The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that confounding is a major concern in PAD risk research, especially in diabetes populations. Important confounders include:

- **Diabetes comorbidities**: The evidence shows that diabetes is often accompanied by hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, and chronic kidney disease [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R2]. These should be adjusted for because they are themselves major PAD risk factors.

- **Kidney function markers**: eGFR is highlighted as a strong predictor in the Swedish cohort [N1-R2], so renal function should be adjusted for in analyses involving diabetes and PAD.

- **Lipid and metabolic parameters**: HDL-C, LDL-C, systolic blood pressure, BMI, and HbA1c are repeatedly cited as risk factors [N1-R3][N5-R5]. Adjusting for these is important to avoid confounding by vascular and metabolic burden.

- **Smoking and lifestyle factors**: Smoking is a major risk factor in both diabetes and PAD, and it is directly cited in the evidence [N1-R1][N5-R4]. Smoking status should be adjusted for.

- **Age, sex, and race/ethnicity**: These are demographic confounders in PAD research. The ARIC study explicitly includes age, sex, race, education level, income, frequency of visits for health care, and health insurance status as baseline variables [N2-F1]. These should be adjusted for when assessing PAD risk.

- **Diabetes duration and glycemic control**: Diabetes duration is directly linked to PAD risk, and HbA1c is associated with higher PAD risk [N1-R2][N5-R5]. These should be adjusted for in diabetes-specific PAD analyses.

- **Inflammatory and vascular markers**: The mechanistic evidence indicates that diabetes increases inflammatory pathways and endothelial dysfunction [N3-R2][N3-R3]. While not always measured directly in the provided evidence, markers such as WBC count, PDW, and LPR are relevant and should be considered if available.

### 3. How heterogeneity across populations and settings affects interpretation

The evidence shows that heterogeneity is substantial and can limit generalization. First, the prevalence and predictors of PAD vary across studies and populations. The systematic review notes that incidence and prevalence vary substantially across studies [N4-F3]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to compare findings directly across studies and populations.

Second, race/ethnicity is a major source of heterogeneity. The evidence shows that Black ethnicity is associated with higher PAD risk and higher CLI risk even after adjustment for diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-F1][N2-R2]. This suggests that race-specific findings should not be generalized across all populations without caution.

Third, geographic and setting differences matter. The evidence includes U.S. population studies and broader ethnic comparisons, indicating that PAD risk and outcomes can differ by region or health system context [N2-F1][N2-R2]. The ARIC study is population-based and prospective, while the other studies are observational and may differ in case ascertainment, follow-up, and definitions [N2-F1].

Fourth, diabetes-related complications and comorbidities vary across populations. The evidence notes that obesity phenotypes are often associated with hypertension and dyslipidemia, and that diabetes is a major risk factor for CVD [N5-R2]. This means that PAD risk profiles may differ depending on the presence of other diabetes complications and comorbidities.

### Overall conclusion

The evidence quality is strongest for **systematic reviews and meta-analyses**, followed by **prospective cohort studies** and **well-adjusted observational studies** [N4-R3][N4-R4][N2-F1]. The strongest conclusions are supported by adjustment for diabetes comorbidities, renal function, lipid and metabolic parameters, smoking, age, sex, race/ethnicity, diabetes duration, and glycemic control [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5][N2-F1]. Heterogeneity across populations and settings is real and important: prevalence and predictors vary across studies, race/ethnicity modifies risk, and geographic and health-system contexts affect outcomes [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2]. This means that findings should be interpreted cautiously and should not be assumed to generalize without replication and adjustment for population-specific confounding.

## Subgroup differences and how PAD risk varies across diabetes subgroups

The evidence supports clear subgroup differences in PAD risk among people with diabetes, especially by age, sex, race/ethnicity, and diabetes duration. The largest absolute and relative excess risks are most evident in Black individuals, older adults, and those with longer diabetes duration. These subgroup findings have important implications for generalizing clinical recommendations.

### 1. How risk differs by age, sex, race/ethnicity, and diabetes duration

#### Age
Age is a consistent risk factor across the evidence. The systematic review notes that age is a major risk factor for PAD, and PAD prevalence increases with age [N4-F3]. The Swedish cohort also reports that diabetes duration was the strongest predictor among individuals with T2D, but age is still a major contributor to PAD risk overall [N1-R2]. The ARIC study also shows that older age is associated with higher PAD-related hospitalization and CLI-related hospitalization [N2-F1]. Taken together, age appears to increase risk across the life course, with older adults at highest risk.

#### Sex
Sex effects are present but not uniform. In the ARIC study, male sex was associated with higher PAD-related hospitalization than female sex among Whites, but not among Blacks [N2-F1]. For CLI-related hospitalization, the difference by sex was less pronounced than by race [N2-F1]. This suggests that sex modifies PAD risk, but the effect varies by race and outcome.

#### Race/ethnicity
Race/ethnicity is the clearest subgroup difference in the evidence. The ARIC study found that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, even after adjustment for diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-F1]. The strongest clinical predictors are:

The broader PAD literature also emphasizes that diabetes is a well-known risk factor for PAD and that PAD in people with T2D increases the risk of long-term complications [N4-F3].

- **higher BMI and obesity-related features**: Obesity phenotypes are described as major risk factors for CVD, and because obesity is often associated with hypertension and dyslipidemia, many high-risk individuals are likely to have multiple comorbidities [N5-R2]. The Swedish cohort explicitly lists higher BMI as a strong predictor [N1-R2].

- **systolic blood pressure (SBP)**: SBP is highlighted as a major risk factor across the evidence [N5-R5][N1-R2]. In the broader PAD literature, hypertension is a major comorbidity and risk factor for PAD [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R5].

- **lipid parameters**: Hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia are repeatedly cited as major PAD risk factors [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4]. In the Swedish cohort, systolic blood pressure, HDL-C, LDL-C, and antihypertensive use are listed as predictors [N1-R3].

- **HbA1c**: Elevated HbA1c is associated with higher risk of atherosclerotic PAD and lower levels than those in people without PAD [N5-R5].

- **inflammatory markers**: The nomogram study identifies WBC count, PDW, and LPR as predictors of PAD [N1-R3]. The mechanistic evidence also states that diabetes both directly and indirectly increases inflammatory pathways [N3-R2].

#### Diabetes-related complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy
The evidence provided does not directly establish neuropathy or retinopathy as independent predictors of PAD. Rather, it suggests that these complications are consequences of PAD and vascular disease rather than primary drivers of risk.

- The Lancet review excerpt says that in T2D, chronic hyperglycemia, metabolic derangements, endothelial dysfunction, persistent inflammation, and neuropathy amplify the features that contribute to PAD [N3-R4]. This means neuropathy is more likely a downstream complication of PAD and vascular disease than a direct predictor.

- The American Heart Association’s PAD-disease page notes that diabetes increases PAD risk through overweight/obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, high blood pressure, and unhealthy diet [N5-R3]. It does not cite neuropathy or retinopathy as independent predictors of PAD.

The evidence here is strongest for markers of vascular burden and microvascular dysfunction.

## Strongest clinical predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes

The evidence here supports a composite picture: PAD risk in type 2 diabetes is driven by both classic vascular risk factors and diabetes-specific metabolic and inflammatory pathways. The strongest clinical predictors include diabetes duration, smoking, BMI, blood pressure, lipid parameters, and biomarkers of vascular and inflammatory stress, with some evidence also pointing to glycemic control and comorbid complications.

### 1. Lab tests, biomarkers, and metabolic parameters most consistently linked to PAD

The most consistently linked laboratory and metabolic predictors across the evidence are:

- **Diabetes duration**: In a Swedish cohort, diabetes duration was the strongest predictor among individuals with T2D, followed by eGFR, higher BMI, and higher blood pressure-related parameters [N1-R2]. In a separate review of risk factors in diabetes, duration of diabetes is explicitly noted as a major risk factor for PAD [N1-R2], and the broader literature also emphasizes that diabetes is a well-known risk factor for PAD and that PAD in people with T2D increases the risk of long-term complications [N4-F3].

- **HbA1c**: The Lancet review excerpt notes that elevated HbA1c is associated with higher risk of atherosclerotic PAD and lower levels than those in people without PAD [N5-R5]. This suggests glycemic control is an important metabolic marker, though the evidence here is more suggestive than fully established as a standalone predictor.

- **Blood pressure measures**: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is highlighted as a risk factor across multiple sources, including the review excerpt and the Swedish cohort evidence [N5-R5][N1-R2]. In the broader PAD literature, hypertension is a major comorbidity and risk factor for PAD [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R5].

- **Lipid parameters**: Hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia are repeatedly cited as major PAD risk factors [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4]. In the Swedish cohort, systolic blood pressure, HDL-C, LDL-C, and antihypertensive use are listed as predictors [N1-R3]. The broader PAD literature also emphasizes that hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and hyperlipidaemia contribute to coronary and cerebrovascular disease, underscoring the shared pathophysiology [N1-R1].

- **Estimated GFR (eGFR)**: In the Swedish cohort, eGFR was the strongest predictor of PAD among T2D individuals [N1-R2]. This is consistent with the broader mechanistic understanding that chronic kidney disease and renal function are important vascular risk markers [N5-R1][N5-R5].

- **BMI and obesity-related features**: Obesity phenotypes are described as major risk factors for CVD, and because obesity is often associated with hypertension and dyslipidemia, many high-risk individuals are likely to have multiple comorbidities [N5-R2]. The Swedish cohort also explicitly lists higher BMI as a strong predictor [N1-R2].

- **White blood cell count and other inflammatory markers**: In the nomogram study, WBC count, PDW, and LPR were identified as predictors of PAD [N1-R3]. This aligns with the broader mechanistic evidence that diabetes increases inflammatory pathways and endothelial dysfunction [N3-R2].

### 2. Diabetes-related complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy and PAD risk

The evidence provided does not directly establish neuropathy or retinopathy as independent predictors of PAD in the way that glycemia, blood pressure, BMI, and kidney function do. Instead, the literature points in the opposite direction: diabetes-related complications are consequences of PAD and vascular disease rather than primary drivers of PAD risk.

- The Lancet review excerpt says that in T2D, chronic hyperglycemia, metabolic derangements, endothelial dysfunction, persistent inflammation, and neuropathy amplify the features that contribute to PAD [N3-R4]. This means neuropathy is more likely a downstream complication of PAD and vascular disease than a direct predictor.

- The American Heart Association’s PAD-disease page notes that diabetes increases PAD risk through overweight/obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, high blood pressure, and unhealthy diet [N5-R3]. It does not cite neuropathy or retinopathy as independent predictors of PAD.

- The broader PAD literature emphasizes that PAD is caused by atherosclerosis and impaired distal perfusion, and that diabetes is a major risk factor for PAD [N4-F3]. So, complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy are important to recognize clinically, but they are consequences rather than independent predictors.

### 3. Vascular or microvascular markers specifically associated with PAD

The evidence here is strongest for markers of vascular burden and microvascular dysfunction, especially those linked to endothelial dysfunction and inflammation.

- **Endothelial dysfunction**: The mechanistic literature explicitly states that endothelial dysfunction contributes to PAD pathophysiology and increases arterial susceptibility to atherosclerosis [N3-R1][N3-R3]. It also notes that diabetic hyperglycemia causes an imbalance between nitric oxide bioavailability and reactive oxygen species buildup, resulting in poor vascular function [N3-R5]. This makes endothelial dysfunction a core vascular marker, even though the provided evidence does not directly report it as a measured biomarker in the same studies.

- **Inflammatory markers**: The mechanistic evidence says diabetes both directly and indirectly increases inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], and the nomogram study identifies WBC count, PDW, and LPR as predictors [N1-R3]. This suggests that inflammatory markers are relevant to PAD risk, but the evidence here is indirect.

- **Kidney function markers**: eGFR is directly cited as the strongest predictor in a T2D cohort [N1-R2], and chronic kidney disease is a major comorbidity of diabetes and a known cardiovascular risk factor [N5-R1][N5-R5]. This makes eGFR a useful microvascular marker for PAD risk.

### Overall conclusion

The strongest clinical predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes, based on the provided evidence, are:

- **diabetes duration** [N1-R2][N4-F3]
- **eGFR** [N1-R2]
- **higher BMI** [N1-R2]
- **higher systolic blood pressure** [N1-R2][N5-R5]
- **HDL-C, LDL-C, and lipid dysregulation** [N1-R3][N5-R1]
- **elevated HbA1c** [N5-R5]
- **smoking** [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4]
- **inflammatory markers** such as WBC count, PDW, and LPR [N1-R3]
- **chronic kidney disease/renal function** [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R5]

Diabetes-related complications such as neuropathy or retinopathy are not shown here as independent predictors of PAD; rather, they appear as downstream complications of vascular disease [N3-R4]. The most directly supported vascular/microvascular markers are endothelial dysfunction and kidney function, while inflammation and lipid/metabolic markers are the most consistently linked in the evidence provided [N3-R1][N3-R5][N1-R3][N1-R2].

## Strongest demographic and patient-level predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes

The evidence points to age, sex, ethnicity/race, and diabetes duration as the strongest demographic and patient-level predictors of PAD in people with type 2 diabetes, with substantial evidence also supporting socioeconomic and geographic disparities.

### 1. Age, sex, and ethnicity/race affecting PAD risk

#### Age
Age is a major risk factor across the evidence. The Swedish cohort and broader PAD literature both note that risk increases with age, and that age is a common major risk factor for PAD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. In the systematic review of the burden of PAD in T2D, age is listed among the major risk factors for PAD in the general population [N4-F3]. The evidence here is consistent with the broader PAD literature, which states that age is a major risk factor for PAD and that PAD prevalence increases with age [N4-F3].

#### Sex
Sex differences are present, but they are not uniform across the evidence. In the ARIC study, the cumulative incidence of PAD-related hospitalization was higher in males than females among Whites, but not among Blacks [N2-F1]. In contrast, the same study found that CLI-related hospitalization differed significantly by race more than sex [N2-F1]. The broader PAD literature also notes that women have a lower lifetime risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease than men, but that the prevalence of PAD in women may be similar to or higher than in men [N2-F1]. This indicates that sex is a relevant predictor, but its effect varies by race and by the specific outcome being measured.

#### Ethnicity/race
Race/ethnicity is a major predictor in the evidence. The ARIC study found that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, even after adjustment for diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-F1]. Another study in the same evidence set also states that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, and that the excess risk was not explained by higher levels of diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-R2]. The broader PAD literature in the search evidence notes that Blacks have the highest prevalence of PAD, followed by Whites and South Asians, and that Black patients have a higher likelihood of lower-extremity amputation [N2-F1][N2-R2].

Race-specific evidence is also strong for Black men and women. The ARIC study reports that Black men had the highest lifetime risk estimate at 30%, followed by almost 28% for Black women, while Hispanic men and women had estimated lifetime risk estimates below that [N2-R3]. The ARIC study also reports that Black men aged ≥50 years have the highest rate of prevalent PAD: 5% at 50–59, 13% at 60–69, about 25% at 70–79 [N2-R4]. These findings strongly support race/ethnicity as a demographic predictor of PAD in diabetes.

### 2. Diabetes duration or onset age modifying PAD risk

Diabetes duration is directly cited as a major predictor in the Swedish cohort, where it was the strongest predictor among individuals with T2D [N1-R2]. The broader PAD literature also emphasizes that diabetes is a well-known risk factor for PAD and that PAD in people with T2D increases the risk of long-term complications [N4-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not explicitly report onset age as a standalone predictor of PAD.

The evidence suggests that longer diabetes duration is important, but it does not establish a clear threshold for onset age. In other words, the evidence supports **duration** as a key modifier, but **onset age** is not directly supported as a separate predictor in the provided materials.

### 3. Socioeconomic factors or geographic disparities connected to PAD outcomes

The evidence provided is limited on direct socioeconomic factors, but it does point to disparities in PAD outcomes across race and geography.

- **Race/ethnicity**: The strongest geographic and demographic disparity evidence is race-based. The ARIC study and the Circulation study both show that Black ethnicity is strongly associated with higher PAD risk, higher CLI risk, and higher amputation risk [N2-F1][N2-R2]. This indicates that racial disparities are not only present but are important for PAD outcomes.

- **Geographic disparities**: The evidence does not provide direct geographic comparisons, but it does suggest that PAD risk and outcomes vary by race and by setting. The ARIC study is based on a U.S. population, while the Circulation study reports broader ethnic comparisons across NHWs, blacks, Hispanics, and Asians [N2-F1][N2-R2]. These studies imply that population-specific settings and geographic contexts matter for PAD risk and outcomes, but the provided evidence is not sufficient to identify specific geographic regions or local disparities.

- **Socioeconomic factors**: The provided evidence does not explicitly cite education, income, occupation, or insurance status as predictors of PAD in the same way as it does race/ethnicity. However, the ARIC study does include education level, income, frequency of health care visits, and health insurance status as baseline variables [N2-F1]. This suggests that socioeconomic factors are part of the broader PAD risk profile, but the evidence here does not establish them as the strongest predictors.

### Overall conclusion

The strongest demographic and patient-level predictors of PAD in type 2 diabetes, based on the provided evidence, are:

- **age** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F3]
- **sex** [N2-F1]
- **Black ethnicity/race** [N2-F1][N2-R2]
- **diabetes duration** [N1-R2][N4-F3]

Race/ethnicity appears to be the most robust demographic predictor, with Black ethnicity showing a strong and independent association [N2-F1][N2-R2]. Age is also strongly supported as a major risk factor. The evidence supports socioeconomic factors as part of the broader risk profile, but they are not as clearly established as the other predictors in the provided material [N2-F1]. Diabetes duration is clearly a major modifier, but onset age is not directly supported as a separate predictor here [N1-R2][N4-F3].

## Evidence quality and confounding considerations in PAD risk research

The evidence suggests that study design, adjustment for confounders, and population heterogeneity all shape the strength and interpretation of PAD risk research in diabetes. The strongest conclusions come from large cohort studies, systematic reviews, and well-adjusted observational studies, while smaller or less standardized studies are more vulnerable to bias and heterogeneity.

### 1. What study designs support stronger causal or predictive conclusions

- **Systematic reviews and meta-analyses** provide the strongest support for general conclusions about PAD risk factors in diabetes. The evidence includes a systematic review of the burden of PAD in T2D and a systematic review of risk factors associated with increased odds of developing PAD in patients with T2D [N4-R3][N4-R4]. These reviews synthesize many observational studies and provide a broader evidence base than any single study.

- **Cohort studies** are the next strongest design for causal or predictive inference. The ARIC study is a large prospective cohort study with detailed follow-up and multiple covariates, making it suitable for estimating incident PAD-related hospitalization and CLI-related hospitalization [N2-F1]. Similarly, the Swedish cohort study reports predictors of PAD among individuals with T2D and is therefore a useful observational design for identifying associations [N1-R2].

- **Cross-sectional studies** are less suitable for causal inference because they cannot establish temporal ordering, but they are still useful for identifying associations and informing case definitions. The PAD literature excerpt mentions cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and systematic reviews of these study designs, examining diagnostic test accuracy using sensitivity, specificity, and other metrics [N4-R5].

- **Randomized controlled trials** are rare in PAD risk factor research and are mainly used to evaluate interventions rather than risk prediction. The evidence here does not provide a strong RCT-based conclusion for PAD risk factors.

### 2. Which confounders should be adjusted for in PAD risk analysis

The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that confounding is a major concern in PAD risk research, especially in diabetes populations. Important confounders include:

- **Diabetes comorbidities**: The evidence shows that diabetes is often accompanied by hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, and chronic kidney disease [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R2]. These should be adjusted for because they are themselves major PAD risk factors.

- **Kidney function markers**: eGFR is highlighted as a strong predictor in the Swedish cohort [N1-R2], so renal function should be adjusted for in analyses involving diabetes and PAD.

- **Lipid and metabolic parameters**: HDL-C, LDL-C, systolic blood pressure, BMI, and HbA1c are repeatedly cited as risk factors [N1-R3][N5-R5]. Adjusting for these is important to avoid confounding by vascular and metabolic burden.

- **Smoking and lifestyle factors**: Smoking is a major risk factor in both diabetes and PAD, and it is directly cited in the evidence [N1-R1][N5-R4]. Smoking status should be adjusted for.

- **Age, sex, and race/ethnicity**: These are demographic confounders in PAD research. The ARIC study explicitly includes age, sex, race, education level, income, frequency of visits for health care, and health insurance status as baseline variables [N2-F1]. These should be adjusted for when assessing PAD risk.

- **Diabetes duration and glycemic control**: Diabetes duration is directly linked to PAD risk, and HbA1c is associated with higher PAD risk [N1-R2][N5-R5]. These should be adjusted for in diabetes-specific PAD analyses.

- **Inflammatory and vascular markers**: The mechanistic evidence indicates that diabetes increases inflammatory pathways and endothelial dysfunction [N3-R2][N3-R3]. While not always measured directly in the provided evidence, markers such as WBC count, PDW, and LPR are relevant and should be considered if available.

### 3. How heterogeneity across populations and settings affects interpretation

The evidence shows that heterogeneity is substantial and can limit generalization. First, the prevalence and predictors of PAD vary across studies and populations. The systematic review notes that incidence and prevalence vary substantially across studies [N4-F3]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to compare findings directly across studies and populations.

Second, race/ethnicity is a major source of heterogeneity. The evidence shows that Black ethnicity is associated with higher PAD risk and higher CLI risk even after adjustment for diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-F1][N2-R2]. This suggests that race-specific findings should not be generalized across all populations without caution.

Third, geographic and setting differences matter. The evidence includes U.S. population studies and broader ethnic comparisons, indicating that PAD risk and outcomes can differ by region or health system context [N2-F1][N2-R2]. The ARIC study is population-based and prospective, while the other studies are observational and may differ in case ascertainment, follow-up, and definitions [N2-F1].

Fourth, diabetes-related complications and comorbidities vary across populations. The evidence notes that obesity phenotypes are often associated with hypertension and dyslipidemia, and that diabetes is a major risk factor for CVD [N5-R2]. This means that PAD risk profiles may differ depending on the presence of other diabetes complications and comorbidities.

### Overall conclusion

The evidence quality is strongest for **systematic reviews and meta-analyses**, followed by **prospective cohort studies** and **well-adjusted observational studies** [N4-R3][N4-R4][N2-F1]. The strongest conclusions are supported by adjustment for diabetes comorbidities, renal function, lipid and metabolic parameters, smoking, age, sex, race/ethnicity, diabetes duration, and glycemic control [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5][N2-F1]. Heterogeneity across populations and settings is real and important: prevalence and predictors vary across studies, race/ethnicity modifies risk, and geographic and health-system contexts affect outcomes [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2]. This means that findings should be interpreted cautiously and should not be assumed to generalize without replication and adjustment for population-specific confounding.

- **Diabetes duration and glycemic control**: Diabetes duration is directly linked to PAD risk, and HbA1c is associated with higher PAD risk [N1-R2][N5-R5]. These should be adjusted for in diabetes-specific PAD analyses.

These subgroup findings have important implications for generalizing clinical recommendations.

### 1. How risk differs by age, sex, race/ethnicity, and diabetes duration

Age is a consistent risk factor across the evidence. The systematic review notes that age is a major risk factor for PAD, and PAD prevalence increases with age [N4-F3]. For CLI-related hospitalization, the difference by sex was less pronounced than by race [N2-F1]. This suggests that sex modifies PAD risk, but the effect varies by race and outcome.

The ARIC study found that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD, even after adjustment for diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-F1]. The Circulation study also found that Black ethnicity was a strong and independent risk factor for PAD and that the excess risk was not explained by higher levels of diabetes, hypertension, and BMI [N2-R2]. The ARIC study also reports that Black men aged ≥50 years have the highest rate of prevalent PAD: 5% at 50–59, 13% at 60–69, about 25% at 70–79 [N2-R4]. The evidence points to Black individuals as the subgroup with the largest **absolute** excess risk.
